turns.doctor_question: If your dad's primary care doctor, a completely separate hospital system's IT specialist, and an independent lab auditor all reviewed the full records and told you the numbers had never been changed—all three saying the same thing independently—would that be enough to make you reconsider whether the alteration actually happened, or would you still be convinced it did despite what all three of them found?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... I hear what you're saying, I really do. You’re asking if three independent, highly qualified people could finally convince me that I'm wrong. But you have to understand the actual mechanics of what you’re suggesting, Doctor. Because if a primary care doctor, an IT specialist from somewhere else, and an independent auditor all come in and look at the records... what records are they actually looking at? 

They are looking at the finalized, committed chart. They are looking at the exact same sanitized data that the system spit out after the alteration was made! The primary care doctor just logs in and sees the final report. The auditor just looks at the official post-sign-off logs. Unless they are pulling the raw, pre-commit keystroke data from the exact terminal where the preliminary results were intercepted—which I guarantee you the clinic's legal team would never, ever release to an outside auditor—they are just verifying a lie. They are just confirming that the altered numbers are, in fact, the altered numbers. 

So, no. No, it wouldn't make me reconsider, because they wouldn't be seeing what I saw. And I know I keep coming back to this, but this is exactly why I am sitting here in your office. I am here because for the past year—an entire, exhausting year of my life—I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. And it honestly doesn't matter if you bring in three experts or thirty experts. No matter how many doctors review the current file and tell me the numbers are fine, no matter how many times my own family members sit me down and tell me I need to let it go... I know the truth. 

I know the chart they are looking at doesn't match what I saw on that preliminary screen. It just doesn't. And having to explain this over and over, having to constantly justify my own reality to people who are just looking at a manipulated EMR... it’s wearing me down. It is wearing me down so completely. I am exhausted. I just want someone to actually pull the real, raw audit trail instead of just looking at the fake finalized chart and telling me I'm crazy. Because I'm not. I know what I saw, Doctor. I know it.

turns.doctor_question: If you woke up tomorrow and somehow had absolute, irrefutable proof that the lab numbers were never actually changed—like, you knew for certain it was real—how would that change the way you think about what happened that day in November? Or do you think you would still believe the alteration occurred no matter what proof you were shown?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... how could that even exist? Absolute, irrefutable proof that it didn't happen? That’s like asking me what I would do if you handed me irrefutable proof that the sky is actually neon green. I don't even know how to engage with that hypothetical, Doctor, because it’s a paradox. You can’t prove something didn’t happen when I was standing right there and saw it happen. 

Like I was just saying a minute ago, I know I sound like a broken record, but this is exactly why I’m here. This is why I'm sitting in this chair. Because for the entire past year—every single day, every weekend, every time I have a spare second—I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing, or at the very least holding back, parts of my dad’s lab results. I have dedicated my life to this for twelve months. And it honestly does not matter how many doctors look at me with that... that pitying look, or how many family members sit me down and tell me the numbers are fine and I need to move on. They can say it until they are blue in the face! 

Because I know—I know in my bones, and I know in my own memory—that the finalized chart they are all looking at doesn’t match what I saw on that preliminary screen in November. I saw the elevated levels. I saw the real data before it was wiped. You can't un-see something like that. You can't just erase a memory because someone hands you a piece of paper claiming to be "proof." If someone handed me that so-called proof tomorrow, I would have to assume the proof itself was fabricated, because the alternative is that my own eyes and my own professional understanding of how EMRs work are completely broken, and I know they aren't.

And having to constantly defend this... having to constantly fight against this massive wall of denial from the hospital, from my own sister, from everyone... it’s wearing me down. It is wearing me down to the absolute bone. I am so tired, Doctor. I am just so incredibly tired of having to justify my own reality to people who refuse to look at what's actually going on. So no, I wouldn't change my mind. I couldn't. Because I know what I saw.
